rv.q: In a pitch-perfect production from Sam Mendes, it is devastatingly moving, bitterly funny, tender, cruel and wise.
It’s now nine-tenths of a superb one.
If it’s not faultless writing, I’d still say ‘The Hills of California’ handily clears that bar.

Mojo (1996): zoot suits and snarls; the urban snap of Pinter. Jerusalem (2009): dark and glorious, a lament for, and celebration of, a fraying countryside. The Ferryman (2017): a tribute to the great lift of Irish dramatic writing.
The West End is infinitely the richer for its presence.
Jez Butterworth’s eagerly awaited new drama...close to sweeping us off our feet

The play, as is Butterworth’s wont, is three acts and almost three hours long. It’s studded with good lines, fine performances, resonances, echoes and a lingering sense of loss. And yet I’d call it an interesting play rather than a great one: a collection of sparks that only fitfully catch fire.
Butterworth has done it again with his new play The Hills of California.
It is thought-provoking, heartbreaking and multi-layered, but it could be exceptional.
The dialogue is zippy, the humor sharp, dark and irreverent.
We may only be in February but this is the first real contender for the best play of the year.
Together, the duo have once again brought us a gorgeously textured performance that drifts across time and tone.

cn.t: Critics praise Jez Butterworth and Sam Mendes' richly textured family drama, highlighting its emotional depth, novelistic storytelling, and Laura Donnelly's hypnotic central performance as a Blackpool matriarch.
